title: Concurrent input slicing & stream tiering - PoC notes
content:
Summary:

This note captures a proof-of-concept design for overlapping prefill and decode work across concurrent streams by: 1) slicing large inputs into parallelizable units, 2) assigning streams to latency tiers, and 3) introducing a lightweight KV-cache lease and eviction signal so decode can safely reuse prefill state without stalling emitter-critical traffic. Goal is to reduce tail latency for interactive streams while preserving throughput for background/batch style workloads.

Context / motivation:
- We frequently see a tension: long prefill (very long prompts, tool outputs, embeddings) blocks GPU kernel availability and causes interactive decode streams to suffer high tail latency.
- Existing approaches (strict separation of prefill and decode queues, simple priority queues) either waste GPU cycles or create unfairness.
- Microbatching helps throughput but obscures real-time QoS for low-latency streams.

High-level idea:
- Break inbound requests into "slices" for prefill stage that can be executed incrementally (input-chunk prefill). Each slice produces KV delta fragments that are mergeable.
- Maintain a tiny per-model "lease map" in the serving runtime that marks which KV epochs are safe to reuse for decode streams. Leases are cheap tokens with short TTLs (50-500ms) and precedence semantics.
- Streams are assigned a runtime tier: realtime (human-facing, low token budget), interactive (bot-to-bot, medium), background (batch/embeddings, tolerant). Scheduler uses tier + estimated remaining prefill to decide whether to:
  * accelerate prefill slice on dedicated kernel (when possible),
  * pause prefill and preempt for a decode slot, or
  * spill prefill state to host memory and resume later.

Components (PoC):
1) Input Slicer
- API: slice(request) -> list(slice_id, token_range, metadata)
- Heuristic: target slice size by tokens (e.g., 64–256) and by alignment to attention-window boundaries. For very large prefix templates (few-k tokens), prefer coarser slices to reduce merge overhead.
- Slices can be prefetched to device sequentially; decoder attach can begin when the first N slices complete or when an explicit decode-start marker is present in the prompt tokens.

2) Microbatch Reorder Buffer (MRB)
- Accepts prefill slices and decode tokens. Provides ordering guarantees per-stream but allows out-of-order execution across streams to improve kernel utilization.
- Each MRB entry: {stream_id, slice_id, state_ref, priority_tier, ready_ts}
- Reordering window is bounded (e.g., 20ms) to limit tail amplification. If slice remains unscheduled beyond window, scheduler inflates its priority.

3) KV Lease Map
- Lease record: {model_id, epoch_id, owner_streams[], ttl_ms, eviction_hint}
- When a prefill slice runs, it writes KV fragments to device memory and publishes a lease for that epoch. A decode stream that wants to reuse that KV must check for active lease; if owned and lease TTL sufficient, decode reuses KV.
- If lease conflicts (multiple competing prefill writers), scheduler serializes or creates copy-on-write KV shards.
- Eviction hints are emitted if memory pressure increases; decode streams can elect to snapshot or continue with partial cache.

4) Kernel Affinity and Fast-paths
- Kernel catalog maintains tags: {prefill, decode, small-seq, large-seq, kv-update}
- Runtime places accelerated prefill-slices that are KV-light onto kernels that can overlap with decode via CUDA streams that do not block inference kernels (where hardware supports concurrent kernel execution).
- Fast-path: for short interactive prefill (<=32 tokens), collapse into a single fused prefill+decode kernel when model and device support it, bypassing MRB.

Admission control and tiering policy:
- Each incoming request is scored: S = alpha * tier_priority - beta * estimated_prefill_time + gamma * remaining_tokens
- Tier_priority: realtime=100, interactive=50, background=0 (configurable)
- If S above threshold, request gets decode-slowpath reserved slot (small equidistant window), otherwise it enqueues as normal.

Fallback semantics:
- If prefill slow and realtime decode arrives: either preempt prefill, merge partial KV into a "warm cache" snapshot for the decode, or migrate prefill to host memory + release device memory. Choice depends on memory pressure and SLA.
- Default: preempt prefill slices at slice granularity and capture partial KV as temporary read-only mapping for decode.

Metrics we will track (PoC):
- p50/p95/p99 latency for realtime vs interactive vs background requests
- Preemption count: how often prefill was interrupted
- KV reuse hit rate (per epoch)
- Memory thrash: device eviction events per minute
- Microbatch utilization: average kernel occupancy and fraction of kernels doing mixed workload (prefill+decode)

Experiment plan (small scale):
- Phase 1: synthetic workload with 3 classes of streams (10% realtime, 30% interactive, 60% background). Run against an Llama-variant model with 32k context emulation (simulate by long prefill tokens).
  * Baseline: current queueing model (no slice overlap).
  * Variant A: input-slicing + MRB, no KV leases (naive reuse).
  * Variant B: add KV leases and slice-aware preemption.
- Primary signal: reduce p99 latency for realtime without >5% throughput loss for background.
- Phase 2: run on real production traces (anonymized) with multiple models, tune alpha/beta/gamma and slice sizes.

Prototype APIs (runtime-level):
- submit_request(request_id, model, prompt, tier_hint) -> assigned_slices[]
- slice_complete(slice_id, device_state_ref, kv_epoch_id, mem_usage)
- request_resume(request_id)  // invoked when prefill completes or decode begins
- lease_query(model, epoch_id) -> {active:boolean, ttl_ms:int, owner_count:int}

Open questions / known risks:
- Merge cost: merging many small KV fragments may be more expensive than running a larger contiguous prefill. Need benchmarks to find knee point.
- Copy-on-write KV costs could blow memory if many competing streams write similar context. Consider delta-compression or summarization heuristics.
- Temporal fairness: background workloads may suffer starvation if slice sizes are too small and realtime streams constantly preempt. Must ensure long-term fairness windows.
- Correctness across model variants and quantized kernels: some kernels have restrictions that make slice fusion impossible. Need cataloging and gating.

Implementation TODOs / short list:
- [ ] Implement input slicer and small unit tests (token alignment, edge cases).
- [ ] MRB skeleton + scheduler hook that can pick-by-tier.
- [ ] Simple in-memory KV-lease map for PoC with TTL and eviction hinting.
- [ ] Microbench: measure merge cost vs monolithic prefill for 128/512/2048 token prefill sizes.
- [ ] Add metrics to runtime dashboard and a tracing label for lease events.

Notes to self / brainstorming fragments:
- Maybe a hybrid: allow some prefill slices to be "speculative decode-ready" — compute the minimal KV that decode needs (last N layers) and keep rest lazily.
- Could piggyback short background slices onto idle decode kernels during tail periods.
- Consider making lease eviction a cooperative call: long-running background tasks get a soft "we will evict in 200ms" signal to checkpoint.

References and prior art:
- Internal: RFC-2024-06-kv-epoching (contains KV shard layout ideas)
- Research notes: "incremental transformer caching" paper notes (internal PPT)
- PR: github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/487 (scheduler hooks)

Acceptance criteria for PoC:
- Demonstrated reduction in p99 for realtime by >=30% on synthetic load without >7% background throughput drop.
- KV reuse hit rate >65% for reuseable epochs in mixed traffic tests.
- No correctness regressions: final outputs must match baseline when requests are executed end-to-end (allowing non-determinism from parallelism).

If the PoC looks good, next steps: productionize lease map in the control plane, expose tier hints in API, run canary on Dedicated cluster.

- Priya
